cards.hook: What separates people who learn fast from people who just study a lot?
p: Metacognition is knowing what you know and how you are doing: monitoring your understanding, then deciding what to do about it. The term comes from psychologist John Flavell in the 1970s.
Learners who check their own understanding as they go, and change tactics when it is not working, tend to do better than those who simply put in hours.
cards.ex: Halfway through a chapter you realize you cannot say what the last page was about. You stop, go back, and explain it out loud in your own words before moving on.
cards.k: Learning has two jobs: doing it, and noticing how it is going.

q.q: Which of these is metacognition?
o: Re-reading a page a fourth time
Noticing you could not explain a page, then changing how you study
q.w: Metacognition is monitoring your own understanding and acting on what you find. Time spent and repetition alone are not it.

cards.src: Flavell, 1979; Dunlosky & Metcalfe, 2009

cards.hook: Why does re-reading feel like learning when it mostly is not?
p: When text is familiar it feels easy, and easy feels like knowing. But recognizing a page is far weaker than being able to produce its content from memory.
Researchers call this an illusion of competence: confidence rises with re-reading even when later recall barely does.
cards.ex: You re-read your notes three times and everything looks obvious. Then the exam gives you a blank page, and the obvious parts are not there.
cards.k: Familiar is not the same as learned.

q.q: Which is the better test of whether you have learned something?
o: Does it feel easy when I read it again?
Can I explain it with the book closed?
Did I highlight the key parts?
q.w: Retrieving it with no help is what an exam, or real life, asks for. How easy something looks while you can see it is a poor guide.

cards.src: Koriat & Bjork, 2005; Karpicke, Butler & Roediger, 2009

b: Closing the book and trying to recall

cards.hook: Why is pulling an answer out of memory worth more than putting it in again?
p: Each time you retrieve something, you strengthen the memory and make it easier to retrieve later. In a well-known experiment, students who practiced recalling a passage remembered more a week later than students who re-read it.
The re-readers felt more confident. The quizzed students actually knew more.
cards.ex: Instead of re-reading a chapter summary, close it and write down everything you can recall. Then check what you missed.
cards.k: Test yourself early and often; the struggle is the strengthening.

q.q: A week after studying, who tends to remember more?
q.w: Roediger and Karpicke (2006) found recall practice beat re-reading at a delay, even though re-reading felt better.

cards.src: Roediger & Karpicke, 2006, Psychological Science

viz.note: Illustration of the pattern, not the exact data

cards.h: Spread it out: the spacing effect
cards.hook: Why does the same hour of study work better split across days?
p: The same amount of study, spread over several sessions, produces longer-lasting memory than doing it all at once. A review of hundreds of results found the best gap depends on how long you need to remember: the longer the goal, the longer the gap.
Cramming works for tomorrow and fails for next month.
cards.ex: Learning vocabulary for a trip in two months: ten minutes on each of six different days beats one hour on a single evening.
cards.k: Several short sessions beat one long one for anything you want to keep.

q.q: You have six hours to learn something you need in a month. What works best?
o: Spread across several days, with review
Skim it all once and trust your memory
q.w: Spacing study produces stronger long-term retention than massing the same time into one session.

cards.src: Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted & Rohrer, 2006, Psychological Bulletin

viz.note: Illustration of the pattern, not the exact data

cards.hook: How fast do we forget what we just learned?
p: In the 1880s Hermann Ebbinghaus memorized lists of nonsense syllables and tested himself at intervals. Forgetting was steepest right after learning, then levelled off.
The exact rate depends on the material and how you review it; meaningful material is forgotten more slowly than nonsense. A modern replication confirmed the overall shape.
cards.ex: A talk you heard this morning feels clear. By tomorrow you recall the main point and a couple of details; a month on, mostly the gist.
cards.k: Forgetting is fastest at first, which is exactly when a quick review pays off.

q.q: When is forgetting steepest?
q.w: The curve drops quickly at first and then flattens, so early review recovers the most.

cards.src: Ebbinghaus, 1885; Murre & Dros, 2015, PLOS ONE

viz.note: Illustration of the shape, not exact figures

cards.hook: Why does mixed practice feel worse and work better?
p: Practicing different kinds of problems mixed together, rather than one kind at a time, makes you work out which method fits each one. That is what real tests and real life ask of you.
In one study of math practice, mixed practice scored lower during the practice itself but about three times higher on a test a week later.
cards.ex: Learning tennis: twenty forehands, then twenty backhands, then twenty serves feels smooth. Mixing them feels clumsy but trains you to pick the right shot.
cards.k: If practice feels slightly clumsy because you must choose, it is probably working.

q.q: Mixed (interleaved) practice usually…
o: Feels harder but helps later performance
q.w: Interleaving makes practice feel worse, but it improves your ability to choose the right method later.

cards.src: Rohrer & Taylor, 2007, Instructional Science

a: AAA BBB CCC: smooth, feels good
b: ABC ABC ABC: harder, lasts longer

cards.hook: When is struggling the whole point?
p: Robert Bjork’s term for conditions that make learning feel slower but help it last: spacing, testing yourself, mixing topics and explaining things in your own words.
Not every difficulty is desirable. It has to be a challenge you can overcome with effort; if it is too hard, you just fail.
cards.ex: Trying to answer a question before the teacher explains it often makes the explanation stick better, even when your guess is wrong.
cards.k: Aim for effortful but doable. Easy and smooth often means shallow.

q.q: Which is a “desirable difficulty”?
o: Studying with the answers in view
Testing yourself before you feel ready
Making the material impossible to follow
q.w: Retrieval attempts are effortful but doable, and they strengthen memory. A difficulty you cannot overcome is just an obstacle.

cards.src: Bjork, 1994; Bjork & Bjork, 2011

cards.hook: Why does trying an answer before you know it help you remember it?
p: Information you produce yourself is remembered better than information you only read; this is the generation effect. Even a wrong guess before the answer can help: studies of “pre-testing” found that failed attempts prepared people to learn the right answer.
The attempt makes you notice what you did not know.
cards.ex: Before reading about a new idea, write down what you think it is. Then read, and compare.
cards.k: Make a guess before you look; being wrong first can help.

q.q: Why can a wrong guess before the answer help learning?
o: It prepares you to notice and encode the right answer
q.w: Attempting an answer, even a wrong one, engages memory and makes the correct answer more meaningful when it arrives.

cards.src: Slamecka & Graf, 1978; Kornell, Hays & Bjork, 2009

cards.hook: Are you as right as you feel? Find out.
p: Calibration means your confidence matches your accuracy: when you say you are 90% sure, you are right about nine times in ten. Most people are overconfident, especially on hard questions.
Try the quick quiz below: mark each statement true or false, then say how sure you are.
cards.ex: A forecaster who says “70% chance of rain” should see rain on about seven of every ten such days. That is being well calibrated.
cards.k: Confidence is a feeling. Track it against results to learn how far to trust it.

q.q: What does being well calibrated mean?
o: Your confidence matches how often you are right
q.w: A calibrated person who says 80% is right about 80% of the time.

cards.src: Lichtenstein, Fischhoff & Phillips, 1982; Moore & Healy, 2008

cards.hook: Do the least skilled really think they are experts?
p: In 1999 Kruger and Dunning reported that people who scored lowest on tests of logic, grammar and humor overestimated their standing most: the bottom quarter, scoring around the 12th percentile, put themselves near the 62nd.

But the popular version, “unskilled people think they are geniuses”, goes further than the evidence. Part of the pattern shows up in any noisy measure, and everyone is imperfect at judging themselves.
cards.ex: Someone new to chess cannot see the moves they are missing, so they have no way to judge how strong their play is.
cards.k: We all misjudge our skill. The gap is widest where we know least, but it is not a law of stupidity.

q.q: What is a fair summary of Dunning–Kruger?
o: Incompetent people are sure they are brilliant
Low performers overestimate themselves, partly for statistical reasons
q.w: The original finding is real, but critics show some of it comes from regression to the mean and the better-than-average effect.

cards.src: Kruger & Dunning, 1999; Gignac & Zajenkowski, 2020, Intelligence

viz.note: Bottom-quarter group, as reported in the 1999 paper

cards.hook: How many things can you hold in mind at once?
p: Working memory holds only a few items at a time. George Miller’s 1956 paper made “seven, plus or minus two” famous; later work suggests the limit for separate chunks is closer to four.
Chunking packs several items into one meaningful unit, which is why 1-9-4-5 is easier to hold as “1945”. Try the digit test below.
cards.ex: The letters F B I C I A are six items, or two chunks if you know them as FBI and CIA.
cards.k: You cannot hold much, so group things into meaningful chunks and write the rest down.

q.q: What does chunking do?
o: Packs several items into one meaningful unit
q.w: Working memory capacity stays small; chunking lets each slot carry more by using meaning you already have.

cards.src: Miller, 1956; Cowan, 2001, Behavioral and Brain Sciences

cards.h: Words plus pictures, when the picture helps
cards.hook: Do diagrams really help you learn?
p: People often learn more from words plus a relevant picture than from words alone. Allan Paivio’s dual coding theory and Richard Mayer’s multimedia learning research support this.
The picture has to carry meaning, such as a diagram of the process. Decorative images and busy slides can get in the way.
cards.ex: To learn how a heart pumps blood, a labelled diagram of the four chambers with arrows for the flow teaches more than a paragraph alone.
cards.k: Use pictures that show how the parts relate. Skip the decoration.

q.q: Which picture helps learning most?
o: A stock photo that matches the topic
A diagram showing how the parts connect
q.w: Explanatory diagrams help because they show structure. Decorative images add load without adding meaning.

cards.src: Paivio, 1986; Mayer, 2009, Multimedia Learning

a: A diagram that shows how the parts connect
b: A decorative picture that adds nothing

cards.hook: Are you a visual learner? The evidence says it will not matter.
p: People do have preferences, such as liking pictures or liking to listen. But a major review found no good evidence that teaching to a person’s preferred style improves how much they learn.
What helps nearly everyone is matching the method to the material: diagrams for shapes, practice for skills, retrieval for facts.
cards.ex: A “visual learner” studying a language still needs to hear and say the words, because the task is about sound.
cards.k: Choose the method for the subject, not for a “style”.

q.q: What did the review of learning styles find?
o: Matching style to teaching boosts learning for most people
No convincing evidence that matching helps
Auditory learners learn best from lectures
q.w: Pashler and colleagues (2008) found no adequate evidence that matching instruction to a preferred style improves learning.

cards.src: Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer & Bjork, 2008, Psychological Science in the Public Interest

a: Teach to your style and you learn more
b: Teach to the subject; style does not predict results

cards.hook: Which popular study habits are almost useless?
p: A large review rated ten common techniques. Practice testing and spaced practice were rated high utility. Highlighting, re-reading and summarizing came out low, partly because they feel productive without doing much.
Self-explanation and mixing problem types were rated moderate.
cards.ex: Swap a color-coded highlighting session for ten minutes of questions you write and answer from memory.
cards.k: Prefer methods that make you retrieve. Be wary of ones that feel smooth.

q.q: Which technique was rated high utility?
q.w: In the review, practice testing and distributed practice were the two techniques rated high utility.

cards.src: Dunlosky, Rawson, Marsh, Nathan & Willingham, 2013, Psychological Science in the Public Interest

viz.note: Utility ratings from the 2013 review

cards.hook: How can you find the holes in what you think you understand?
p: Explaining an idea step by step in plain words, to yourself or to someone else, shows you where your understanding is thin. Research on self-explanation finds that students who explain material as they study learn it more deeply.
It is sometimes called the Feynman technique, after the physicist, though the method itself is simply self-explanation and teaching.
cards.ex: Try explaining how a vaccine works to a ten-year-old. Wherever you wave your hands, you have found something to relearn.
cards.k: If you cannot explain it simply, you have found what to study next.

q.q: What is explaining an idea in plain words good for?
o: Finding gaps in your own understanding
q.w: Self-explanation exposes missing steps and builds connections between ideas.

cards.src: Chi, Bassok, Lewis, Reimann & Glaser, 1989; Chi et al., 1994

cards.hook: What one question deepens almost any fact?
p: Asking yourself “why would this be true?” and answering it ties a new fact to what you already know. Studies of elaborative interrogation found better memory for facts when learners generated explanations.
It works best when you already know something about the topic.
cards.ex: You learn that the Moon always shows the same face to Earth. Ask why: tides have slowed its spin until one rotation takes as long as one orbit.
cards.k: Turn every fact into a “why” and answer it.

q.q: Elaborative interrogation works by…
o: Linking a new fact to what you already know
q.w: Generating a reason connects the fact to existing knowledge, which makes it easier to retrieve.

cards.src: Pressley, McDaniel, Turnure, Wood & Ahmad, 1987; Dunlosky et al., 2013

s: Link it to what you know

cards.h: Brain training mostly trains the game
cards.hook: Do brain games make you smarter?
p: Practice improves the exact task you practice, and sometimes close cousins. But a large review of the brain-training literature concluded that evidence these games improve broader thinking in everyday life is weak.
Learning transfers best when the new situation shares structure with the old one, and when you practiced across varied examples.
cards.ex: Playing a memory game daily makes you better at that game, not necessarily better at remembering names.
cards.k: Practice the thing you want to get better at, in varied forms.

q.q: What does the evidence on brain training suggest?
o: It improves the trained task more than everyday thinking
q.w: Gains tend to stay close to the practiced tasks; broad transfer has not been convincingly shown.

cards.src: Simons et al., 2016, Psychological Science in the Public Interest

cards.hook: Does 10,000 hours of practice make you an expert?
p: Anders Ericsson found that top violinists had spent more hours in focused, feedback-driven practice. The “10,000 hours” figure was a rough average from that study, popularized by Malcolm Gladwell, not a rule.
A later review found practice explained a modest share of differences in performance, varying a lot by field.
cards.ex: An hour of focused piano practice on the hard bars, with feedback, beats three hours of playing through what you already know.
cards.k: How you practice matters more than the hour count. Practice helps; it is not the whole story.

q.q: What does “deliberate practice” involve?
o: Focused work on weaknesses, with feedback
q.w: Ericsson defined it as effortful, goal-directed practice on specific weaknesses, with feedback.

cards.src: Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Römer, 1993; Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald, 2014

viz.note: Share of differences in performance explained by practice, 2014 review

cards.h: Growth mindset: what the evidence says
cards.hook: Does believing you can improve actually make you improve?
p: Carol Dweck’s idea is that believing abilities can grow helps people persist and learn. Large studies find the average effect is small: a broad meta-analysis found only a weak link between mindset and achievement, with larger effects for students under the most strain.
A big national trial found a short online lesson raised grades slightly among lower-achieving students.
cards.ex: “I cannot do math” is a belief that can steer how much you try. Changing the belief helps a little; changing your study methods helps more.
cards.k: Mindset helps modestly. Pair it with better methods and supportive conditions.

q.q: What do large studies find about growth mindset?
o: A small average effect, larger for some groups
q.w: Sisk and colleagues (2018) found weak overall effects; Yeager and colleagues (2019) found modest gains for lower-achieving students.

cards.src: Sisk, Burgoyne, Sun, Butler & Macnamara, 2018; Yeager et al., 2019, Nature

cards.h: Judge your learning after a pause
cards.hook: When is your sense of “I know this” most trustworthy?
p: Right after studying, material is fresh in short-term memory, so it feels known. Nelson and Dunlosky found that judging how well you know something is much more accurate if you wait a while first, because you then test what is really stored.
So delay your self-check, and base it on trying to recall, not on how familiar the page looks.
cards.ex: Study a list of facts, do something else for twenty minutes, then quiz yourself. That score tells you what you will actually remember.
cards.k: Check what you know after a delay; just-studied feels falsely solid.

q.q: When are judgments of learning most accurate?
o: After a delay, based on trying to recall
q.w: A delay forces retrieval from long-term memory, so your judgment reflects what you actually retained.

cards.src: Nelson & Dunlosky, 1991, Psychological Science

viz.note: Illustration of the gap, not exact data

cards.hook: Why do we look for evidence that we are right?
p: We tend to seek, notice and remember information that fits what we already believe. In Peter Wason’s 1960 puzzle, people shown the sequence 2-4-6 guessed the rule and then tested only examples that fit their guess, so they rarely discovered they were wrong.
Try the puzzle below, then notice how you went about it.
cards.ex: After deciding a colleague is unreliable, you remember every missed deadline and forget the many times they came through.
cards.k: Test your belief by looking for what would prove it wrong.

q.q: What is the best way to test a belief?
o: Collect examples that agree with it
Look for cases that could show it is false
q.w: A test that can only confirm tells you little. Cases that could contradict the idea are the informative ones.

cards.src: Wason, 1960; Nickerson, 1998, Review of General Psychology

cards.hook: Why does the first number you hear stick to your own guess?
p: When estimating something uncertain, people start from a number they have just seen and adjust too little. Tversky and Kahneman spun a rigged wheel before asking people to guess the share of African countries in the United Nations.
People who saw a low number guessed a median of 25%; those who saw a high number guessed 45%, though the wheel was obviously random.
cards.ex: A shop shows a crossed-out higher price, and the sale price feels like a bargain even if it was never the real price.
cards.k: Before you accept a number, ask where it came from, and make your own estimate first.

q.q: What is anchoring?
o: Settling on the average of all the numbers you have seen
Estimates being pulled toward an earlier number, even a random one
q.w: An irrelevant starting number can drag a later estimate toward it, as the rigged wheel showed.

cards.src: Tversky & Kahneman, 1974, Science

viz.note: Median guesses in the 1974 study

cards.hook: Why do the vivid risks feel bigger than the real ones?
p: We judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Dramatic, recent or heavily reported events are easy to picture, so they feel more common than they are.
In surveys, people have overestimated deaths from vivid causes such as accidents and tornadoes and underestimated deaths from quiet ones such as diabetes and stroke.
cards.ex: After seeing news of a plane crash, flying feels risky for a while, though driving to the airport is statistically the more dangerous part.
cards.k: When a risk feels big, ask how often it really happens, not how easily you can picture it.

q.q: The availability heuristic makes us…
o: Judge likelihood by how easily examples come to mind
q.w: Ease of recall stands in for frequency, and vivid or well-reported events are easy to recall.

cards.src: Tversky & Kahneman, 1973; Lichtenstein, Slovic, Fischhoff, Layman & Combs, 1978

b: Heart disease, diabetes: feel rarer than they are

cards.hook: What are you not seeing when you only see the winners?
p: We study what survived and forget what did not. In the Second World War, the statistician Abraham Wald was asked where to add armour to bombers. The planes that returned showed bullet holes in certain places, but he reasoned that the holes marked where a plane could be hit and still make it home.
The armour belonged where the returning planes were not hit.
cards.ex: Stories of successful founders who dropped out ignore the far larger number who dropped out and failed, whom nobody writes about.
cards.k: Ask what happened to the cases you cannot see.

q.q: What was Wald’s insight?
o: Armour the places with most holes
The missing planes were hit where the survivors were not
q.w: Planes hit in the unmarked places never came back, so those places needed protection.

cards.src: Mangel & Samaniego, 1984, Journal of the American Statistical Association (on Wald’s work)

a: Planes that returned, with holes in some places

cards.hook: Why do we keep going because of what we have already spent?
p: A sunk cost is time or money already spent that cannot be recovered. It should not affect what you do next, but it often does: people continue with a poor choice to avoid “wasting” what they put in.
In one study, people who had paid full price for season theatre tickets attended more shows than those who got a discount, though the seats were identical.
cards.ex: You keep watching a boring film because you paid for it. Leaving costs nothing more; staying costs another two hours.
cards.k: Ask only: from here, what is the best use of my next hour or pound?

q.q: Which should affect a decision about what to do next?
o: What each option will cost and give from now on
How embarrassed you would be to quit
q.w: Past, unrecoverable costs are the same whatever you choose. Only future costs and benefits differ between options.

cards.src: Arkes & Blumer, 1985, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

cards.hook: Can the wording of a choice change what you pick?
p: Tversky and Kahneman asked people to choose between two programs to fight a disease expected to kill 600. Described as “200 people will be saved”, most people took the sure option. Described as “400 people will die”, most took the gamble, though the outcomes were identical.
About 72% chose the sure option when framed as gains, and about 22% when framed as losses.
cards.ex: A medicine described as “90% survive” sounds safer than the same medicine described as “10% die”.
cards.k: Restate a choice in the opposite frame before you decide.

q.q: What does the framing effect show?
o: People weigh identical outcomes differently depending on wording
q.w: Describing the same outcomes as gains or as losses changed which option people preferred.

cards.src: Tversky & Kahneman, 1981, Science

viz.note: Share choosing the sure option, 1981 study

cards.hook: Why does everything seem obvious after it happens?
p: Once we know an outcome, we overestimate how predictable it was and misremember what we thought before. Baruch Fischhoff showed this in 1975: people told an event’s result judged it as having been more likely than those who were not told.
This is the “I knew it all along” feeling.
cards.ex: After a relationship ends, the warning signs look so clear that you wonder how you missed them, though at the time they were mixed in with many other signals.
cards.k: Write predictions down beforehand so you can learn from what you actually knew.

q.q: What is hindsight bias?
o: Believing an outcome was more predictable once you know it
q.w: Knowing the result distorts our memory of what was foreseeable.

cards.src: Fischhoff, 1975, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance

cards.hook: Why does everything take longer than we plan?
p: People underestimate how long their own projects will take, even when they know similar ones ran late. In a study of students writing a thesis, the average prediction was about 34 days, their worst-case guess was about 49, and the real average was about 56.
We plan from the best-case story, not from how such projects usually go.
cards.ex: Your estimate for sorting the paperwork is two hours. Last time it took six, and the time before, five.
cards.k: Base your estimate on how long similar things actually took, not on the plan.

q.q: A better way to estimate a task is to…
o: Look at how long similar tasks took before
Add ten percent to your first guess
q.w: Using the record of similar past projects, called reference-class forecasting, corrects for the best-case story we tell ourselves.

cards.src: Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

viz.note: Students’ thesis completion times, 1994 study

cards.hook: Why does a terrible day tend to be followed by a better one?
p: Results contain luck. Very high or very low results are partly luck, so the next result tends to be closer to average, with no cause needed.

Daniel Kahneman noticed flight instructors who believed shouting at trainees after a bad landing worked, and praise after a good one backfired. Performance after a bad landing would improve anyway, and after a great one would slip.
cards.ex: You feel dreadful, try a new remedy, and feel better the next day. Part of that was probably the usual drift back toward your normal.
cards.k: Before crediting a cause for a change from an extreme, ask what would have happened anyway.

q.q: Why do extreme results tend to be followed by less extreme ones?
o: Because the cause has run out
Because extremes include luck that does not repeat
q.w: Extreme outcomes tend to include unusual luck, so the next draw tends to land closer to the average.

cards.src: Galton, 1886; Kahneman, 2011, Thinking, Fast and Slow

viz.note: Illustration of the pattern

cards.hook: Can a trend in every group reverse when you combine the groups?
p: Sometimes the overall figure points one way while each subgroup points the other. In 1973 the University of California, Berkeley admitted about 44% of male applicants and about 35% of female applicants overall, which looked like bias against women.
Within most departments, women were admitted at similar or higher rates. Women had applied more to the departments that were hardest to get into.
cards.ex: A treatment can look worse overall than another only because it was given to sicker patients.
cards.k: Before trusting a headline average, ask how the groups differ and look inside them.

q.q: What explained the Berkeley pattern?
o: Women did worse in every department
Applicants differed in which departments they applied to
q.w: The mix of departments differed between men and women, so the overall rates misled.

cards.src: Bickel, Hammel & O’Connell, 1975, Science

b: Women similar or higher in most

cards.hook: Can a detailed story seem more likely than a plain one?
p: Tversky and Kahneman described Linda, a bright, outspoken philosophy graduate concerned with social justice. Asked whether she is more likely a bank teller or a bank teller who is active in the feminist movement, most people chose the second.
That cannot be right: a group within a group can never be larger than the group that contains it.
cards.ex: “A flood causing thousands of deaths” can seem more likely than “a flood”, because the first comes with a story.
cards.k: Extra details make a story more vivid, never more probable.

q.q: Which is always at least as likely?
q.w: Every case of A and B is also a case of A, so A alone is at least as probable as A and B together.

cards.src: Tversky & Kahneman, 1983, Psychological Review

viz.o: Every feminist bank teller is also a bank teller

cards.hook: Do you really know how a zip works?
p: People feel they understand everyday things such as zips, toilets and bicycles far better than they do. Rozenblit and Keil asked people to rate their understanding, then to write out a step-by-step explanation, and their ratings dropped afterwards.
Trying to explain exposes how much of “knowing” is a feeling of familiarity.
cards.ex: You are sure you understand how your tax or your phone works, until a child asks “but how?” a third time.
cards.k: Test your understanding by explaining it step by step, out loud or on paper.

q.q: What happened when people tried to explain how a device works?
o: They realized they understood less than they thought
q.w: Writing the explanation revealed gaps, so their self-ratings fell.

cards.src: Rozenblit & Keil, 2002, Cognitive Science

cards.hook: Why do we pick holes in evidence we dislike?
p: People do not weigh evidence evenly. We tend to accept welcome conclusions on thin evidence and demand more from unwelcome ones. Ziva Kunda described this as reasoning that serves a goal.
Smart people are not immune; they can build better arguments for what they already believe.
cards.ex: A study that backs your view looks well designed; one that does not looks “biased” and you start hunting for flaws.
cards.k: Ask yourself: if this evidence pointed the other way, would I accept it?

q.q: A good check on motivated reasoning is…
o: Apply the same standard whichever way the evidence points
q.w: Holding both welcome and unwelcome findings to the same standard reduces the bias.

cards.src: Kunda, 1990, Psychological Bulletin; Taber & Lodge, 2006

cards.h: Does a correction make people dig in?
cards.hook: Do facts make people believe the myth more?
p: The “backfire effect” is the claim that correcting a false belief strengthens it. The early studies were influential, but later large studies found it to be rare. Across 52 issues, one study found that people mostly updated in the right direction when shown facts.
Corrections work, usually modestly, and attitudes can stay put even when beliefs shift.
cards.ex: Showing a friend a clear source about a myth tends to nudge their belief, even if their politics do not change.
cards.k: Do not give up on facts; expect small shifts, not conversions.

q.q: What do large studies find about the backfire effect?
o: It is rare; corrections usually help a little
q.w: Wood and Porter (2019) found essentially no backfire across a wide range of topics.

cards.src: Wood & Porter, 2019, Political Behavior

a: Facts make people dig in harder
b: Corrections nudge beliefs the right way, a little

cards.hook: How can you see a plan’s weak spots before it fails?
p: Before starting, imagine the project has already failed and write down why. Gary Klein calls this a pre-mortem. Giving people permission to imagine failure makes it easier to voice worries.
An early experiment on “prospective hindsight” found that imagining an outcome as already happened helped people come up with more reasons for it.
cards.ex: Before moving house, you imagine it is a year later and it went badly. Maybe the commute was awful, or you could not afford the rent. Now you can check both.
cards.k: Ask “it failed; why?” while you can still change the plan.

q.q: A pre-mortem asks you to…
o: Review a project after it ends
Imagine it has failed and list the reasons
q.w: Imagining failure as already happened prompts more and better reasons than asking what might go wrong.

cards.src: Mitchell, Russo & Pennington, 1989; Klein, 2007, Harvard Business Review

cards.h: Fast and slow thinking: what held up
cards.hook: Do we have two minds, a quick one and a careful one?
p: Daniel Kahneman popularized describing thinking as a fast, automatic mode and a slow, effortful one. The idea is a useful rule of thumb: quick judgments are efficient but prone to predictable errors, and deliberate thinking can catch some of them.
It is a simplification, though. Some of the book’s best-known studies, especially on “priming”, have since failed to replicate, and researchers debate how separate the two modes are.
cards.ex: Spotting a face is instant. Working out 17 × 24 needs effort. Most of life runs on the quick mode.
cards.k: Slow down for big, unfamiliar decisions; trust practiced intuition only in areas with fast, clear feedback.

q.q: What is the fair takeaway?
o: Quick thinking is efficient but error-prone; take care on big choices
q.w: The two-mode picture is a helpful simplification, but some of its supporting studies have not replicated.

cards.src: Kahneman, 2011, Thinking, Fast and Slow; Doyen et al., 2012, PLOS ONE (a priming replication failure)

cards.hook: Can putting a feeling into words really turn it down?
p: In brain-imaging studies, naming an emotion tended to reduce activity in the amygdala, a region involved in threat, and to raise activity in a part of the prefrontal cortex involved in regulation. Reviews of later work find that labelling feelings often reduces their intensity.
The effect is modest and it varies from person to person.
cards.ex: Instead of “I feel awful”, you stop and say, “I feel disappointed and a bit afraid.” The vague wave of feeling becomes something with edges.
cards.k: Find the more precise word for what you feel.

q.q: What did labelling an emotion tend to do?
q.w: Lieberman and colleagues (2007) found labelling reduced amygdala activity, and later reviews found it often reduces emotional intensity.

cards.src: Lieberman et al., 2007, Psychological Science; Torre & Lieberman, 2018

cards.h: Reappraisal: change the meaning, not the facts
cards.hook: Can a different way of seeing an event change how it feels?
p: James Gross’s research separates two ways of managing emotion. Reappraisal means reinterpreting what a situation means, such as seeing a hard conversation as information rather than a verdict. Suppression means hiding the feeling.
Reappraisal tends to lower the emotion itself. Suppression usually leaves the feeling in place and can cost memory and connection.
cards.ex: A friend does not reply. “They do not care” becomes “They are probably swamped.” Nothing changed outside, but the feeling shifts.
cards.k: Ask: what is another believable way to read this?

q.q: What is the difference between reappraisal and suppression?
o: Reappraisal changes the meaning; suppression hides the expression
q.w: Reappraisal changes how the event is understood; suppression leaves the feeling and tries to hide it.

cards.src: Gross & Levenson, 1993; Gross, 2002, Psychophysiology

cards.h: Step back: the fly on the wall
cards.hook: How can you think about something painful without being swamped?
p: Ethan Kross and colleagues found that reflecting on an upsetting experience from the outside, as if watching from a distance, or speaking to yourself in the third person, tended to reduce emotional reactivity compared with reliving it from the inside.
It helps you make sense of what happened instead of replaying it.
cards.ex: Rather than asking “Why did this happen to me?”, ask “What would I tell a friend in this position? What is going on for them?”
cards.k: Look at it from the outside, then ask what you would say to a friend.

q.q: Self-distancing means…
o: Viewing it from an outside perspective
q.w: Taking an observer’s view, such as third-person self-talk, tends to lower reactivity while still allowing you to think it through.

cards.src: Kross & Ayduk, 2017, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology

b: Watching it: “what is going on here?”

cards.hook: When does thinking it over stop helping?
p: Susan Nolen-Hoeksema found that repetitive, passive brooding on how bad you feel and why predicts longer and more severe low mood. Reflection, curious and aimed at understanding, is different.
A useful signal: if you are replaying the same thoughts and getting nowhere, you are ruminating. Shifting to “what is one thing I can do?” interrupts it.
cards.ex: Lying awake rehearsing a conversation for the tenth time is rumination. Writing down three things you could do tomorrow is problem-solving.
cards.k: If thinking is circling, switch to a concrete next step or to something absorbing.

q.q: Which is rumination?
o: Going over the same painful thoughts without a new insight
q.w: Rumination is repetitive and passive; it tends to deepen low mood rather than resolve it.

cards.src: Nolen-Hoeksema, Wisco & Lyubomirsky, 2008, Perspectives on Psychological Science

b: A new angle or a concrete next step

cards.hook: Do we really get used to good and bad events?
p: We tend to adapt to changes in our circumstances, so the glow of good news and the sting of bad news both fade. But adaptation is partial and uneven. Long-running studies find that people adapt to some events and not fully to others.
After divorce, for example, life satisfaction on average recovers only partly, and individuals differ widely: some return to where they were, others do not.
cards.ex: A pay rise is thrilling for a month, then it is just your income. A hard loss hurts sharply, then slowly becomes part of the landscape.
cards.k: Expect feelings to shift over time, and expect people to differ in how fast.

q.q: What do long-term studies say about adaptation?
o: It is common but incomplete and varies between people
q.w: Lucas and colleagues found that adaptation to life events is real but partial and highly individual.

cards.src: Brickman & Campbell, 1971; Lucas, 2005, Psychological Science; Lucas, 2007

viz.note: Illustration of a common pattern; paths vary widely

cards.hook: Do we all pass through five stages of grief?
p: The famous five stages (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance) came from Elisabeth Kübler-Ross’s observations of dying patients, not from studies of bereaved people. Research has not supported them as a fixed sequence that everyone follows.
George Bonanno found several common paths, including steady resilience. The dual process model describes swinging between facing the loss and rebuilding life, and both are normal.
cards.ex: On one day you feel fine and busy, the next day it hits you. That swinging is a recognized pattern, not a failure.
cards.k: There is no right order and no deadline.

q.q: What does research say about the five stages?
o: Everyone passes through them in order
They were not shown to be a fixed sequence
q.w: Studies of the bereaved find varied paths, and the stages were never validated as a universal sequence.

cards.src: Bonanno, 2004, American Psychologist; Stroebe & Schut, 1999

a: Five steps, in order, then done
b: Varied paths, swinging back and forth

cards.hook: How do we judge an experience in hindsight?
p: Kahneman and colleagues had people hold a hand in painfully cold water twice: 60 seconds, and 60 seconds plus 30 more as the water was warmed slightly. Most people chose to repeat the longer one, whose ending was less painful, though it contained more pain overall.
We remember the most intense moment and the ending, and largely ignore duration.
cards.ex: A vacation with one wonderful day and a pleasant last evening is remembered fondly even if much of it was dull.
cards.k: End things well, and look at the whole, not just the peak and the end.

q.q: Which parts of an experience dominate memory?
q.w: In the cold-water study, memory followed the worst moment and the final moment, not total duration.

cards.src: Kahneman, Fredrickson, Schreiber & Redelmeier, 1993, Psychological Science

viz.note: Illustration: the peak and the ending are what we remember

cards.h: Loss aversion: how big is it?
cards.hook: Do losses really hurt twice as much as gains please?
p: Kahneman and Tversky’s prospect theory proposed that losses weigh more heavily than equal gains, often described as about twice as much. The idea explains why people hold on to things and turn down fair bets.
Newer work suggests the size varies a lot with the situation and may be smaller than once thought, so treat “twice” as a rough guide.
cards.ex: You decline a coin flip where you win $110 or lose $100, though it is favorable, because the possible loss looms larger.
cards.k: A loss feels bigger than the equal gain, so check whether a choice is wise rather than just comfortable.

q.q: What is loss aversion?
o: Disliking losses more than liking equal gains
q.w: Prospect theory says losses carry more psychological weight than equal gains; the size of the gap varies.

cards.src: Kahneman & Tversky, 1979, Econometrica; Gal & Rucker, 2018

viz.note: Often described as about 2 to 1; the size varies

cards.hook: How much do other people really notice you?
p: We overestimate how much others notice our appearance and mistakes. In one study, students made to wear an embarrassing T-shirt into a room guessed that about half of the people there would notice. Only about a quarter did.
Everyone is busy being the star of their own life, so most people give you far less attention than it feels like.
cards.ex: You replay an awkward comment for days, while the other person has long forgotten it.
cards.k: Assume people notice you about half as much as you fear.

q.q: Compared with their estimates, how many people noticed the T-shirt?
q.w: Participants expected about half to notice; only about a quarter did (Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky, 2000).

cards.src: Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky, 2000, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

viz.note: Embarrassing T-shirt study, 2000

cards.h: How long does a habit take?
cards.hook: Is it really 21 days?
p: The “21 days” figure is a myth. In a study that followed people building a new daily habit, the time to reach automatic behavior ranged from 18 to 254 days, with a typical (median) of 66.
Missing a single day did not derail progress. Simple habits formed faster than complex ones.
cards.ex: A short walk after breakfast becomes automatic sooner than a full workout routine, because there is less to decide each day.
cards.k: Start small, expect weeks to months, and do not let one missed day end it.

q.q: What was the typical time to automaticity in the study?
o: About 66 days, with a wide range
q.w: The median was 66 days; individuals ranged from 18 to 254 days (Lally et al., 2010).

cards.src: Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts & Wardle, 2010, European Journal of Social Psychology

viz.note: Illustration of the typical curve; people range from 18 to 254 days

cards.hook: What small trick makes intentions more likely to happen?
p: Peter Gollwitzer found that turning a goal into a specific plan of the form “If situation X, then I will do Y” makes follow-through much more likely. A meta-analysis of 94 studies found a medium-to-large effect.
The plan hands the decision to the situation: when the cue appears, the action is already chosen.
cards.ex: “If it is 7 p.m. and I am home, I will do ten minutes of stretching” works better than “I will exercise more.”
cards.k: Pick a cue, name the action, and write it as an if–then sentence.

q.q: What makes an “implementation intention”?
q.w: Linking a specific cue to a specific action raises the chance you will act when the cue appears.

cards.src: Gollwitzer, 1999; Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology

cards.hook: Does being kind to yourself make you lazy?
p: Kristin Neff describes self-compassion as treating yourself with the care you would give a friend: recognizing pain, remembering that others struggle too, and not harshly judging yourself. Reviews link it with lower anxiety and depression.
It does not seem to weaken motivation. In one experiment, people who were helped to be self-compassionate after a failure spent longer studying for the next test.
cards.ex: After a mistake, try the words you would use for a friend in your place: “That was hard. Anyone could have found it so. What now?”
cards.k: Speak to yourself as you would to someone you care about.

q.q: What did the experiment find about self-compassion and motivation?
o: It increased motivation to improve after failure
It made no difference at all
q.w: Breines and Chen (2012) found self-compassion increased the time people spent preparing after a failure.

cards.src: Neff, 2003; MacBeth & Gumley, 2012; Breines & Chen, 2012

b: “That hurt. Others stumble too. What next?”

cards.hook: Does self-control run out like fuel?
p: The idea that willpower is a limited resource that gets used up was popular after studies in the late 1990s. But large replication projects, involving many labs, found the effect to be tiny or absent.
What we do know: when tired, hungry or stressed, self-control feels harder, and good habits and setups reduce how much willpower you need.
cards.ex: Putting the cookies out of sight works better than relying on resisting them every evening.
cards.k: Design your surroundings so good choices are easy; do not count on a willpower battery.

q.q: What did big replication studies find about ego depletion?
q.w: A 23-lab replication found an effect near zero, and the original idea is now widely doubted.

cards.src: Baumeister et al., 1998; Hagger et al., 2016, Perspectives on Psychological Science

b: The classic effect did not replicate well

cards.hook: How much does movement really help how you feel?
p: Reviews of trials find that regular exercise tends to reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety, with small to moderate effects, and that even a single bout of activity can lift mood for a while. The size of the benefit is smaller in the most rigorous trials.
It is a helpful tool, not a replacement for treatment when someone needs it.
cards.ex: A twenty-minute walk when you feel flat often shifts your mood, even if only slightly and for a few hours.
cards.k: Movement helps modestly and reliably; use it alongside, not instead of, other support.

q.q: What do the best-designed trials suggest about exercise and depression?
o: A real but smaller benefit than early studies suggested
q.w: Cooney and colleagues (2013) found a moderate effect overall that shrank in the most rigorous trials.

cards.src: Cooney et al., 2013, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews

viz.note: Findings of the 2013 Cochrane review

cards.hook: What predicts a healthy, happy later life?
p: The Harvard Study of Adult Development has followed several hundred men, and later their families, for more than 80 years. Its researchers report that the quality of people’s close relationships was among the strongest predictors of health and well-being later in life.
The sample is small and mostly one group, so it shows an association, not a guarantee. Other long-term research points the same way.
cards.ex: Someone with a few people they could call at 3 a.m. is better placed than someone with a large circle of casual contacts.
cards.k: Time with people who matter is an investment, not a luxury.

q.q: What does this long study suggest?
o: Wealth is the best predictor of health
Close relationships are among the best predictors of well-being
q.w: The study reports relationship quality as one of the strongest predictors, with the caveat that it is observational.

cards.src: Waldinger & Schulz, 2023, The Good Life; Vaillant, 2012

cards.hook: Why do open loops nag at you?
p: Unfinished goals tend to pop back into mind. A set of experiments by Masicampo and Baumeister found that making a specific plan for how to finish a task reduced the intrusive thoughts about it, even before the task was done.
Plans seem to tell the mind the matter is handled, so it can stop checking.
cards.ex: Writing “Tuesday 9 a.m.: call the bank” can quiet the worry about it more than doing nothing or just promising yourself.
cards.k: Write the next step and when you will do it; then let it go.

q.q: What reduced nagging thoughts about an unfinished task?
o: Trying not to think about it
Making a specific plan for it
q.w: Specific plans reduced intrusion in these experiments, even though the task itself was still unfinished.

cards.src: Masicampo & Baumeister, 2011, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

s: Write the next step and when

cards.hook: Is the adult brain fixed?
p: The brain keeps adapting throughout life. In a well-known study, London taxi drivers, who memorize thousands of streets, had a larger posterior hippocampus, a region involved in spatial memory, and the size was related to how long they had been driving.
A later study followed trainees and found changes in those who qualified, though not in those who failed.
cards.ex: Learning a new language or instrument in adulthood is slower than in childhood, but it still changes the brain’s wiring.
cards.k: Practice physically shapes the brain at any age.

q.q: What did the taxi-driver studies show?
o: The hippocampus is fixed in adults
Years of navigating were linked to hippocampal change
Drivers are born with larger hippocampi
q.w: Maguire and colleagues (2000) found a link with experience, and the 2011 trainee study found changes after qualifying.

cards.src: Maguire et al., 2000, PNAS; Woollett & Maguire, 2011, Current Biology

cards.hook: Do we only use ten percent of our brains?
p: This is false. Brain imaging shows activity across the whole brain over a day, damage to almost any area has consequences, and a brain that wasted 90% of its tissue would be an extraordinary evolutionary extravagance.
The brain is only about 2% of body weight but uses roughly 20% of the body’s resting energy.
cards.ex: Even while you sleep, large parts of the brain are busy sorting and storing the day.
cards.k: You already use all of your brain; the question is how to use it well.

q.q: How much of the brain’s energy budget does it use?
o: About 20% of the body’s resting energy
q.w: The brain is around 2% of body mass and uses roughly a fifth of the body’s resting energy.

cards.src: Raichle & Gusnard, 2002, PNAS; Beyerstein, 1999

viz.note: Approximate figures for an adult

cards.hook: Are you a logical left-brainer or a creative right-brainer?
p: The hemispheres do specialize, for example language is usually left-lateralized. But the idea that people are “left-brained” or “right-brained” in personality is a myth. A study of over a thousand brain scans found no sign that people lean on one side’s network.
Nearly every task uses both hemispheres, connected by millions of fibres.
cards.ex: Writing a story uses language areas more on one side and imagery and emotion processing on both; creative work is not just “the right side”.
cards.k: Brains are not left- or right-types; they work as one network.

q.q: What did the large brain-scan study find?
o: No evidence of left- or right-dominant networks in individuals
Creative people use only the right side
q.w: Nielsen and colleagues (2013) found no evidence for individual “left-brain” or “right-brain” network dominance.

cards.src: Nielsen, Zielinski, Ferguson, Lainhart & Anderson, 2013, PLOS ONE

a: Logical left, creative right: you are one type
b: Both sides work together on almost everything

cards.h: Sleep helps you keep what you learned
cards.hook: Does sleeping on it really work?
p: In 1924 Jenkins and Dallenbach found that people recalled more of a list after sleeping than after the same time awake. Modern research suggests sleep helps consolidate memories, including by replaying them and strengthening important ones.
It is not magic, and the details are still being worked out, but a rested brain generally remembers better.
cards.ex: Studying in the evening, sleeping, then quizzing yourself in the morning usually beats staying up late to cram.
cards.k: Protect sleep after learning; it is part of studying.

q.q: Why does sleep help learning?
q.w: Research since Jenkins and Dallenbach (1924) shows sleep supports memory consolidation.

cards.src: Jenkins & Dallenbach, 1924; Diekelmann & Born, 2010, Nature Reviews Neuroscience

viz.note: Illustration of the pattern, not exact data

cards.h: One bad night and emotions run hot
cards.hook: Why does everything feel worse when you are tired?
p: In an experiment, people who had been kept awake for a night showed about 60% greater amygdala activity in response to upsetting images than people who had slept, along with weaker links to the prefrontal regions that help regulate emotion.
It is one small study, but many others find that poor sleep makes mood and self-control worse.
cards.ex: The same email that is a minor irritation after a good night feels like an insult when you are exhausted.
cards.k: Do not judge big problems at your most tired; sleep first if you can.

q.q: What did sleep loss do in the study?
o: Increased amygdala response to upsetting images
q.w: The sleep-deprived group showed an amygdala response about 60% greater (Yoo et al., 2007).

cards.src: Yoo, Gujar, Hu, Jolesz & Walker, 2007, Current Biology

viz.note: Illustration of the direction of the finding

cards.h: Dopamine is about wanting, not just pleasure
cards.hook: Is dopamine the pleasure chemical?
p: Dopamine is often called the pleasure chemical, but research suggests it is more about prediction and motivation. Wolfram Schultz found that dopamine neurons fire when a reward is better than expected, and then shift to firing at the cue that predicts it.
Kent Berridge’s work separates “wanting” (drive) from “liking” (enjoyment), which can come apart.
cards.ex: The pull to check your phone is wanting: it can draw you back again and again even when checking is not especially enjoyable.
cards.k: Wanting something and enjoying it are different systems.

q.q: What does dopamine most clearly signal?
q.w: Dopamine neurons respond to unexpected rewards and to predictive cues, driving learning and motivation.

cards.src: Schultz, Dayan & Montague, 1997, Science; Berridge & Robinson, 1998

cards.hook: Can you look straight at something and not see it?
p: Simons and Chabris asked people to watch a video of players passing basketballs and count the passes by one team. Midway, a person in a gorilla suit walked through and thumped their chest. About half of the viewers did not notice.
We see what we attend to; attention is narrow, and we are poor at knowing what we are missing.
cards.ex: A driver deep in a phone call can look at a pedestrian and not register them at all.
cards.k: Attention is a spotlight, and what is outside it can be invisible to you.

q.q: About how many viewers missed the gorilla?
q.w: Roughly half of observers busy counting passes did not notice the gorilla (Simons & Chabris, 1999).

cards.src: Simons & Chabris, 1999, Perception

a: What you think you would see
b: What happens when attention is busy

cards.hook: Can you really do two things at once?
p: For tasks that need thought, the brain mostly switches rather than works in parallel, and each switch has a cost in time and errors. Experiments by Rubinstein, Meyer and Evans found time lost with each switch, more so for complex tasks.
Easy or well-practiced tasks, such as walking and chatting, can be combined.
cards.ex: Answering messages while reading a report feels efficient, but you re-read paragraphs and take longer overall.
cards.k: Do one demanding thing at a time, then switch deliberately.

q.q: What does “multitasking” on thinking tasks usually involve?
q.w: Switching takes time and can raise errors, especially for complex tasks.

cards.src: Rubinstein, Meyer & Evans, 2001, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance

cards.hook: How reliable is a vivid memory?
p: Memory reconstructs events each time we recall them, so it can be changed by what we are told afterwards. In a classic study, Loftus and Palmer showed people a car crash and asked how fast the cars were going when they “smashed” or “hit”. “Smashed” produced higher speed estimates.
A week later, about 32% of the “smashed” group reported seeing broken glass, versus about 14% of the “hit” group; there was none.
cards.ex: Two siblings can remember the same family event differently, each sure they are right, since each has reshaped it over years.
cards.k: Vividness and confidence do not guarantee accuracy; check important memories against records.

q.q: What did the wording “smashed” change?
o: Speed estimates and later false memories of glass
Only how fast people said the cars were going
q.w: It raised the speed estimates and increased reports of broken glass that was not there.

cards.src: Loftus & Palmer, 1974, Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior

viz.note: Reports of broken glass a week later, 1974

cards.h: Cells that fire together wire together
cards.hook: What is learning, physically?
p: Donald Hebb proposed in 1949 that when one neuron repeatedly helps to fire another, the connection between them strengthens. The catchy phrase is a later paraphrase. In 1973, Bliss and Lømo discovered long-term potentiation, a lasting strengthening of synapses that matches the idea.
It is a simplification, but it captures why repetition and association build memories.
cards.ex: Pairing a new word with a vivid image fires two sets of neurons together, building a link you can follow later.
cards.k: Learning is the strengthening of connections through use.

q.q: What does Hebb’s idea suggest about practice?
o: Connections strengthen when neurons are active together
q.w: Repeated co-activation strengthens synapses, which is part of how experience shapes memory.

cards.src: Hebb, 1949; Bliss & Lømo, 1973, Journal of Physiology

cards.h: Stress is not always the enemy
cards.hook: Does stress always harm you?
p: Short bursts of the stress response mobilize energy and sharpen attention. Chronic, unrelenting stress is the harmful kind, linked with poorer sleep, mood and memory.
How you read the signs seems to matter too: in one experiment, people told that a racing heart helps performance did better under pressure than those told to calm down.
cards.ex: Before a talk, your heart pounds. Telling yourself “my body is getting ready” can work better than “I must calm down”.
cards.k: Short stress can help; long stress needs recovery.

q.q: What did reframing arousal as helpful do?
o: Helped performance under pressure in that study
q.w: Jamieson and colleagues (2010) found that reappraising arousal as helpful improved performance.

cards.src: Jamieson, Mendes, Blackstock & Schmader, 2010, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology

viz.note: Illustration of the classic inverted U; the exact shape varies

cards.hook: Does caffeine give you energy?
p: Caffeine does not supply energy. While you are awake, a chemical called adenosine builds up and makes you feel sleepy; caffeine blocks the receptors it acts on, so you feel less tired.
The tiredness has not gone, only masked. The half-life of caffeine in the body is about five hours on average, though it varies widely between people.
cards.ex: A coffee at 4 p.m. may still be half-active at 9 p.m., which can delay sleep even if you do fall asleep.
cards.k: Caffeine hides sleepiness; it does not replace sleep.

q.q: What does caffeine do?
o: Blocks the receptors adenosine uses to signal sleepiness
q.w: It blocks adenosine receptors, so the sleepiness signal is dampened rather than removed.

cards.src: Fredholm, Bättig, Holmén, Nehlig & Zvartau, 1999, Pharmacological Reviews

s: Feels less tired; sleep debt remains

cards.hook: Why does morning light matter?
p: Your body has a roughly 24-hour internal clock in the brain’s suprachiasmatic nucleus. Light is its strongest reset signal: morning light tends to advance the clock, and bright light in the evening or night tends to delay it.
That is why late-night screens and bright rooms can push sleep later.
cards.ex: Stepping outside for ten minutes after waking tends to help set your day, even on cloudy days, since outdoor light is far brighter than indoor light.
cards.k: Get bright light early and dim light late.

q.q: Which light timing tends to delay your body clock?
o: Bright light late in the evening
q.w: Evening and night light signal “later” to the clock and can delay sleep.

cards.src: Czeisler et al., 1989; Khalsa, Jewett, Cajochen & Czeisler, 2003, Journal of Physiology

viz.note: Which way light shifts the body clock

cards.hook: Can a walk help you think of new ideas?
p: In experiments by Oppezzo and Schwartz, people generated more creative ideas while walking than while sitting, and the effect lingered a little after they sat down again. It was strongest for open-ended thinking, not for finding the single right answer.
The samples were small, so treat it as promising rather than settled.
cards.ex: Stuck on how to word a letter? A ten-minute walk with no phone often shakes loose a new angle.
cards.k: When you need new ideas, try a walk.

q.q: For which kind of thinking did walking help most?
q.w: Walking improved divergent thinking more than convergent thinking in these experiments.

cards.src: Oppezzo & Schwartz, 2014, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition

cards.hook: Why is it so hard to name the color when the word says another?
p: In 1935 John Ridley Stroop found that people are slower to name the ink color of a word when the word spells a different color, such as the word RED printed in blue. Reading is so practiced that it runs automatically and interferes with naming the color.
It shows how habits of attention compete with what you intend to do. Try the quick test below.
cards.ex: Driving a familiar route on autopilot when you meant to go somewhere new is the same kind of conflict: the habit fires before the intention.
cards.k: Automatic habits can override intentions; attention is what slows them down.

q.q: What slows you down in the Stroop test?
o: An automatic habit (reading) interfering with naming the color
q.w: Word reading is automatic, so it competes with naming the ink color when the two conflict.

cards.src: Stroop, 1935, Journal of Experimental Psychology; MacLeod, 1991, Psychological Bulletin

cards.hook: If sunlight is white, where does the blue come from?
p: Sunlight contains every color. Air molecules scatter short wavelengths such as blue far more strongly than long ones such as red, so blue light is bounced around and reaches your eyes from every part of the sky.

The sky is not violet because the Sun gives out less violet, some is absorbed high up, and our eyes are less sensitive to it. At sunset the light crosses more air, scattering the blue away and leaving the reds.
cards.ex: The same scattering explains red sunsets: low sunlight has so much air to cross that most of the blue is scattered out of the beam.
cards.k: Short wavelengths scatter more, so the daytime sky looks blue and low sunlight looks red.

q.q: Why is the sky blue rather than violet?
o: Violet does not exist in sunlight
The Sun gives less violet, some is absorbed, and eyes see it poorly
q.w: Violet is scattered even more, but the Sun emits less of it, the upper atmosphere absorbs some, and our eyes respond weakly to it.

cards.src: Rayleigh, 1871; Young, 1981, Applied Optics

viz.note: Not to scale

cards.hook: Is summer when the Earth is closest to the Sun?
p: No. The seasons come from the tilt of Earth’s axis, about 23.4 degrees. When your hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, sunlight strikes more directly and days are longer, so it is summer.
In fact Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of the northern winter, and farthest in early July.
cards.ex: When it is summer in London it is winter in Sydney, though both are about the same distance from the Sun.
cards.k: Tilt, not distance, makes the seasons.

q.q: What causes the seasons?
q.w: The axial tilt changes how directly sunlight strikes each hemisphere across the year.

cards.src: NASA Earth Observatory; any introductory astronomy text

viz.note: Axis tilt stays pointed the same way as Earth goes around

cards.h: Looking up is looking back in time
cards.hook: When you look at a star, what are you really seeing?
p: Light takes time to travel. We see the Moon as it was about a second ago, the Sun as it was about eight minutes ago, and the nearest star beyond the Sun as it was a little over four years ago.
The Andromeda galaxy, visible to the naked eye as a faint smudge, is seen as it was roughly 2.5 million years ago.
cards.ex: If the Sun vanished this instant, we would carry on seeing it, and feeling its gravity, for about eight minutes.
cards.k: The sky is a history lesson: farther means older.

q.q: How old is the light we see from the Sun?
q.w: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth.

cards.src: NASA; International Astronomical Union

viz.note: Bar heights show order only; the real gaps are enormous

cards.hook: How does a population change without anyone steering it?
p: Darwin’s idea needs three things: individuals vary, some of that variation is inherited, and some variants leave more offspring than others. Over generations the helpful variants become more common.
It has no goal and no foresight; it only favors what works in the current environment.
cards.ex: When an antibiotic is used, bacteria that happen to resist it survive and multiply, so the next generation is mostly resistant.
cards.k: Variation, inheritance and differing survival add up to change, with nobody in charge.

q.q: Which is NOT needed for natural selection?
o: A goal the species is aiming for
q.w: Selection acts on what already varies; it does not aim at anything.

cards.src: Darwin, 1859, On the Origin of Species

cards.hook: How does a code in a cell become a living body?
p: DNA holds instructions. A gene is copied into RNA, and the RNA is read to build a protein, which does much of the work in cells. Francis Crick called this the central dogma: information flows from DNA to RNA to protein.
Humans have roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes, a small part of the genome.
cards.ex: The protein haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in your blood, is built from instructions in a few genes.
cards.k: DNA is a recipe, RNA is the working copy, and proteins are what get made.

q.q: What is the usual flow of genetic information?
q.w: Genes in DNA are transcribed into RNA, which is translated into proteins.

cards.src: Crick, 1970, Nature; International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2004

cards.h: Where does a tree’s mass come from?
cards.hook: A tree weighs tons. Did it come out of the soil?
p: In the 1600s, Jan Baptist van Helmont grew a willow for five years in a pot of weighed soil, giving it only water. The tree gained about 75 kg while the soil lost only about 57 grams.
He concluded the tree was made of water. We now know most of the dry mass comes from carbon dioxide in the air, which plants turn into sugars using light, with water supplying the hydrogen.
cards.ex: A log that burns away to ash was built mostly from air; the ash left behind is the part that came from the soil.
cards.k: Trees are built largely out of air.

q.q: Where does most of a tree’s dry mass come from?
q.w: Photosynthesis builds sugars from carbon dioxide and water; the carbon in wood is mostly from the air.

cards.src: van Helmont, published 1648; standard plant biology

viz.note: Van Helmont’s willow, approximate figures

cards.hook: Almost every solid sinks in its own liquid. Why not ice?
p: As water freezes, its molecules lock into an open, six-sided lattice held by hydrogen bonds. That arrangement takes up about 9% more space than liquid water, so ice is less dense and floats.
It matters for life: lakes freeze from the top down, and the ice insulates the water below.
cards.ex: A pond can be covered with ice while fish swim beneath it, because the ice stays at the surface instead of sinking.
cards.k: Ice is less dense than water because of the open structure hydrogen bonds create.

q.q: Why does ice float?
o: Its open lattice is less dense than liquid water
q.w: Hydrogen bonds hold molecules in an open arrangement that takes up about 9% more volume than the liquid.

cards.src: Eisenberg & Kauzmann, 1969, The Structure and Properties of Water

b: Open six-sided lattice: about 9% more space, so it floats

cards.h: Entropy and the arrow of time
cards.hook: Why do eggs break but never un-break?
p: Entropy counts how many microscopic arrangements match what you see. Mixed, spread-out states can happen in vastly more ways than ordered ones, so in an isolated system things drift toward the mixed state simply because it is overwhelmingly more probable.
Order can still grow locally if energy flows through. Earth receives concentrated sunlight and radiates the same energy back as spread-out heat.
cards.ex: Milk poured into coffee spreads out and never gathers itself back into a blob, since the mixed arrangements vastly outnumber the unmixed one.
cards.k: Disorder wins by numbers, and that gives time a direction.

q.q: Why does entropy tend to rise in an isolated system?
o: Disordered arrangements are overwhelmingly more probable
q.w: There are vastly more disordered arrangements than ordered ones, so random motion nearly always heads there.

cards.src: Boltzmann, 1877; Schrödinger, 1944, What Is Life?

viz.note: Dots drifting out from a corner: mixed states vastly outnumber ordered ones

cards.hook: Does relativity matter in everyday life?
p: GPS satellites orbit about 20,000 km up. Their clocks run slower because they move fast, by about 7 microseconds a day, and faster because gravity is weaker up there, by about 45 microseconds a day. The net result is about 38 microseconds a day faster than clocks on the ground.
Without correcting for this, position errors would build up at roughly ten kilometers a day.
cards.ex: The next time your map app finds you within a few meters, it is using both of Einstein’s theories of relativity.
cards.k: Relativity is not just theory: it is built into the navigation in your pocket.

q.q: What would happen if GPS ignored relativity?
o: Errors would grow by kilometers every day
q.w: The tiny clock differences, if uncorrected, would add up to roughly ten kilometers of positioning error a day.

cards.src: Ashby, 2003, Living Reviews in Relativity

viz.note: Approximate figures for GPS satellite clocks

cards.hook: Why does a tiny bit of mass hold so much energy?
p: Einstein’s equation says that mass and energy are two forms of the same thing, linked by the speed of light squared, a huge number. A single gram of matter, if completely converted, would release about 90 trillion joules, roughly the energy of about 20 thousand tons of TNT.
In the Sun, fusing hydrogen into helium converts about 0.7% of the mass to energy, and that is what shines on us.
cards.ex: The Sun turns about four million metric tons of its mass into light and heat every second, and has kept this up for billions of years.
cards.k: A little mass is a lot of energy, because of c squared.

q.q: What does E = mc² link?
q.w: It states that a mass m corresponds to an energy of m times the speed of light squared.

cards.src: Einstein, 1905, Annalen der Physik

cards.h: How a vaccine trains the immune system
cards.hook: How can a harmless jab protect you from a dangerous disease?
p: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless piece or copy of a germ, such as a weakened or inactivated version, a fragment, or instructions for making a fragment. The body responds and keeps memory cells ready.
If the real germ arrives later, the response is faster and stronger. Edward Jenner began this in 1796 using cowpox against smallpox, and smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980.
cards.ex: It is a fire drill: the response is rehearsed, so when there is a real fire, people know what to do.
cards.k: Vaccines give the immune system a rehearsal, with no illness.

q.q: What do memory cells do after a vaccine?
o: Respond faster if the real germ arrives
q.w: Memory B and T cells let the immune system react quickly to a germ it has already learned to recognize.

cards.src: Jenner, 1798; WHO, 1980, declaration of smallpox eradication

s: A fast response to the real thing

cards.hook: How did people learn that germs, not bad air, spread disease?
p: In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that more mothers died after childbirth in the ward run by doctors than in the one run by midwives. When he made doctors wash their hands with chlorinated lime, deaths dropped from around one in ten to one or two in a hundred.
In 1854 John Snow mapped cholera deaths in London to a single water pump, and the outbreak ebbed after its handle was removed. Both showed the power of looking closely at the data.
cards.ex: Washing hands with soap remains one of the cheapest, most effective ways to prevent infection.
cards.k: Careful counting beat the theory of “bad air” and saved lives.

q.q: What did Snow’s map of cholera cases show?
o: Cases clustered around one water pump
q.w: The cases clustered around the Broad Street pump, pointing to contaminated water.

cards.src: Semmelweis, 1861; Snow, 1855, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera

a: Doctors’ ward: about 1 in 10 mothers died

cards.h: Plate tectonics: the idea that waited
cards.hook: Why did scientists reject continental drift for fifty years?
p: In 1912 Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had moved, noting how coastlines and fossils match across oceans. Geologists mostly rejected it because he had no mechanism for how continents could plow through the seafloor.

In the 1960s, mapping of seafloor spreading and the magnetic stripes on either side of mid-ocean ridges supplied the evidence. Plates move a few centimeters a year, roughly as fast as fingernails grow.
cards.ex: South America and Africa, which now sit thousands of kilometers apart, are moving apart by a few centimeters a year.
cards.k: A right idea can wait decades for the evidence and mechanism that make it convincing.

q.q: Why was Wegener’s idea first rejected?
q.w: The fit was striking, but without a mechanism for movement many geologists would not accept it.

cards.src: Wegener, 1915; Vine & Matthews, 1963, Nature

cards.h: The table that predicted the future
cards.hook: How did a chart of elements predict elements nobody had found?
p: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the known elements by atomic weight and by chemical behavior. Where the pattern broke, he left gaps and predicted that undiscovered elements would fill them, describing their properties in advance.
Gallium, scandium and germanium were found within about twenty years, matching his predictions closely. In 1913 Henry Moseley showed that atomic number, not weight, is the true order.
cards.ex: The pattern of repeating properties is why lithium, sodium and potassium all react in similar ways.
cards.k: A good model predicts things nobody has seen yet.

q.q: What made Mendeleev’s table so convincing?
o: It was the first list of elements
He predicted missing elements and they were found
q.w: The later discoveries of gallium, scandium and germanium matched his predicted properties.

cards.src: Mendeleev, 1869; Moseley, 1913, Philosophical Magazine

cards.h: Light is a small slice of a huge family
cards.hook: Is visible light a special kind of thing?
p: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all the same thing, electromagnetic waves, differing only in wavelength. Our eyes see just a narrow band, roughly 380 to 750 nanometres.
James Clerk Maxwell worked out in the 1860s that light is an electromagnetic wave, and Heinrich Hertz generated radio waves in 1887.
cards.ex: Your phone, a microwave oven and the sunlight on your skin all use different parts of the same spectrum.
cards.k: Everything from radio to gamma rays is light; we just see a thin slice.

q.q: What distinguishes X-rays from radio waves?
o: They are a different kind of thing
q.w: All electromagnetic waves are the same kind of thing; wavelength (and thus energy) sets the type.

cards.src: Maxwell, 1865; Hertz, 1887

viz.note: Not to scale

cards.hook: How can single particles produce a wave pattern?
p: In the double-slit experiment, particles are sent toward two narrow openings. Even when electrons are fired one at a time, each arrives as a single dot, yet over many electrons the dots build up bands of high and low density, the signature of interference.
Quantum theory describes this with probabilities for where each electron will land. It predicts the pattern extremely well, though how to interpret it is still debated.
cards.ex: It is like a single raindrop landing in one place, while thousands of drops somehow trace out a wave pattern.
cards.k: Quantum objects are not simply little balls or simply waves; the math predicts what we see.

q.q: What builds up when electrons are sent through two slits one at a time?
o: A pattern of bands, like interference
q.w: Individual electrons land as dots, but together they form an interference pattern (Tonomura et al., 1989).

cards.src: Tonomura, Endo, Matsuda, Kawasaki & Ezawa, 1989, American Journal of Physics

s: It lands as a single dot

cards.h: Base rates: the test result that misleads
cards.hook: A test is 80% accurate and you test positive. How worried should you be?
p: Imagine a condition that affects 1 in 100 people, with a test that catches 80% of cases but also gives a false alarm for about 9.6% of healthy people. Of 1,000 people, 10 have it and 8 test positive; of the 990 who do not, about 95 also test positive.
So of roughly 103 positives, only 8 are real: about 8%. These are textbook figures, not those of any real screening test.
cards.ex: When a rare event is tested for, most positives can be false alarms, because there are so many more people without it.
cards.k: A result means little until you know how common the thing was to begin with.

q.q: Why are most positives false alarms in this example?
o: Healthy people vastly outnumber ill ones, so false alarms add up
q.w: The condition is rare, so a small false-alarm rate applied to the large healthy group produces more false positives than true ones.

cards.src: Eddy, 1982; Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, 1995, Psychological Review

g: Do not have it, test positive
viz.note: 1,000 people; textbook figures, not a real screening test

cards.hook: Does p = 0.03 mean there is a 97% chance the effect is real?
p: No. A p-value is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if there were really no effect. It is not the probability that the idea is true, and it says nothing about how large or important an effect is.
In 2016 the American Statistical Association issued a statement warning against treating p below 0.05 as proof.
