cards.ex: A p-value of 0.03 means: if nothing were going on, results like these would turn up about 3 times in 100. That is a surprise, not a certainty.
cards.k: A small p-value means “surprising if nothing is going on”, no more.

q.q: What does a p-value measure?
o: The chance the hypothesis is true
How surprising the data would be if there were no effect
q.w: It is the probability of data this extreme assuming no effect; it is not the probability the hypothesis is true.

cards.src: Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016, The American Statistician

a: The chance your idea is true
b: How surprising the data are if nothing is going on

cards.hook: Why do small studies swing so wildly?
p: Tversky and Kahneman called it the belief in the “law of small numbers”: people expect small samples to look like the population. They do not. Flip a fair coin ten times and a split of 7–3 or more lopsided comes up about a third of the time.
With more flips the share of heads settles near 50%. Small studies, with few people, can show striking effects by luck alone.
cards.ex: Three of your five friends loved a restaurant, so it must be great? Five is far too few to tell.
cards.k: Ask how many were studied before believing a striking result.

q.q: Roughly how often does ten fair flips give 7–3 or a more lopsided split?
o: About a third of the time
q.w: The probability is about 34%, so lopsided results in small samples are common.

cards.src: Tversky & Kahneman, 1971, Psychological Bulletin

viz.note: Illustration: results settle toward 50% as flips increase

cards.hook: After five reds, is black “due”?
p: Independent events have no memory. A fair roulette wheel or coin does not “correct” itself after a run. In a famous 1913 episode at Monte Carlo, the ball reportedly fell on black 26 times in a row, and gamblers lost heavily betting that red was overdue.
Over very many spins the proportions even out, but that happens by dilution, not by correction.
cards.ex: After four heads in a row, the next flip is still 50:50, because the coin cannot know what came before.
cards.k: Chance does not owe you a correction.

q.q: After a run of reds on a fair wheel, the chance of red next time is…
q.w: Each spin is independent of earlier ones, so the odds do not change.

cards.src: Tversky & Kahneman, 1971; Huff, 1959, How to Take a Chance

s: No: the wheel has no memory

cards.hook: How do you compare a risky choice with a safe one?
p: Expected value multiplies each outcome by its probability and adds them up: the average result if you could repeat the choice many times. It is a useful yardstick for bets, insurance and decisions with clear stakes.
It is not the whole story, since a loss you cannot afford matters more than the arithmetic suggests.
cards.ex: A coin flip that pays $3 on heads and costs $2 on tails has an expected value of +50 cents a flip. A ticket costing $2 for a one-in-millions jackpot usually has a negative one.
cards.k: Weigh each outcome by how likely it is, then check what you can afford to lose.

q.q: What is the expected value of winning $3 on heads and losing $2 on tails?
q.w: Half the time you gain $3 and half the time you lose $2: an average of +50 cents per flip.

cards.src: Fermat & Pascal, 1654; Huygens, 1657

cards.h: Compound growth and the rule of 72
cards.hook: How long does money take to double?
p: When growth is added to what has already grown, the curve bends upward. A quick estimate: divide 72 by the yearly growth rate in percent to get the years to double. At 6% a year, about 12 years; at 3%, about 24.
The rule is approximate but good for ordinary rates. The same arithmetic works against you for debts that carry interest.
cards.ex: A balance growing 6% a year takes about 12 years to double, then 12 more to double again, so the second doubling adds far more than the first.
cards.k: Time and the growth rate matter more than you expect; the same math works on debt.

q.q: At 4% a year, about how long does it take to double?
q.w: The rule of 72 gives 72 divided by 4, or about 18 years.

cards.src: Pacioli, 1494 (earliest known mention of the rule); standard arithmetic

viz.note: Illustration of the shape

cards.hook: How many times must you fold a sheet of paper to reach the Moon?
p: Each fold doubles the thickness. A sheet 0.1 mm thick folded 42 times would be over 440,000 km, farther than the Moon at about 384,000 km. Doubling looks slow at first and then explodes.
You cannot actually fold paper that many times; the record for an ordinary sheet is 12 folds, by Britney Gallivan in 2002, using a very long strip.
cards.ex: Early in an outbreak or a debt, numbers look small. Doubling every few days or years makes the later numbers vast.
cards.k: Our minds expect straight lines; check whether something is doubling.

q.q: What does folding paper 42 times show?
q.w: Repeated doubling grows beyond intuition: 0.1 mm doubled 42 times is more than the distance to the Moon, on paper at least.

cards.src: Gallivan, 2002 (the 12-fold record); standard arithmetic

viz.note: Illustration: slow, then explosive

cards.hook: How many people before two probably share a birthday?
p: Surprisingly few. With 23 people the chance that at least two share a birthday is just over 50%; with 40 it is about 89%; with 70 it is about 99.9%. The reason is that you are not comparing one person to the rest but all pairs: 23 people make 253 pairs.
It shows how badly our intuition handles combinations.
cards.ex: In a room of 30, a shared birthday is more likely than not, and it feels like a coincidence only because we think of our own birthday.
cards.k: Count the pairs, not the people.

q.q: How many people give roughly even odds of a shared birthday?
q.w: With 23 people there are 253 pairs, which puts the chance of a match at just over 50%.

cards.src: von Mises, 1939; standard probability

viz.note: Computed values; the curve passes 50% at 23 people

cards.hook: Should you switch doors?
p: You choose one of three doors; behind one is a car, behind the others goats. The host, who knows where the car is, opens a different door to reveal a goat and offers you the chance to switch. Switching wins two times in three.
Your first pick had a one-in-three chance, and the host’s action does not change it. The remaining two-thirds of probability now sits on the one unopened door.
cards.ex: Picture 100 doors: you pick one, and the host opens 98 goat doors. Would you stick with your 1-in-100 pick or swap to the one left?
cards.k: New information changes the odds only for what it can tell you about.

q.q: Should you switch?
q.w: Your first pick stays at 1 in 3; the other door carries the remaining 2 in 3 when the host must reveal a goat.

cards.src: Selvin, 1975, The American Statistician; vos Savant, 1990

viz.note: Chance of winning the car

cards.hook: How do you know a treatment works, not just that people got better?
p: People often improve for reasons unrelated to a treatment: natural recovery, regression to the mean, expectation. A randomized controlled trial gives similar groups the treatment or a comparison by chance, and, ideally, nobody knows who got which.
Randomizing balances the factors we know and the ones we do not, so a difference afterwards can be put down to the treatment.
cards.ex: The 1948 streptomycin trial for tuberculosis is often called the first modern randomized trial: allocation by chance showed a clear benefit.
cards.k: Compare like with like, by chance, and keep everyone blind.

q.q: Why is random assignment powerful?
o: It balances known and unknown differences between groups
It removes the need for a control group
q.w: Chance assignment tends to spread known and unknown factors evenly, so differences can be attributed to the treatment.

cards.src: Medical Research Council, 1948, BMJ; Hill, 1990

cards.h: Significant is not the same as important
cards.hook: If a result is statistically significant, does it matter?
p: Not necessarily. With a large enough sample, a tiny difference can be statistically significant. What matters in practice is the size of the effect. Jacob Cohen’s rough benchmarks for standardized differences are 0.2 for small, 0.5 for medium and 0.8 for large.
He meant them as rough conventions, not laws; what counts as important depends on the context.
cards.ex: A drug that lowers blood pressure by 0.5 points in a trial of 100,000 people may be “significant” and still pointless.
cards.k: Ask two questions: is it real, and is it big enough to matter?

q.q: What does effect size tell you that significance does not?
q.w: Significance addresses chance; effect size addresses how big the difference is.

cards.src: Cohen, 1988, Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences

viz.note: Cohen’s rough benchmarks

cards.hook: Why should one study never settle a question?
p: In 2015 the Open Science Collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology experiments. About 97% of the originals reported a significant result; only about 36% of the repeats did, and the average effect size was about half as large.
This does not mean psychology is worthless. It means single findings are provisional, and well-repeated ones deserve more trust.
cards.ex: A headline saying “a new study finds…” is a starting point. Look for repeated results and larger samples.
cards.k: Trust findings that have been repeated, not just reported.

q.q: What happened when 100 psychology studies were repeated?
o: Far fewer found significant results the second time
q.w: About 36% of the repeats were significant against 97% of the originals (Open Science Collaboration, 2015).

cards.src: Open Science Collaboration, 2015, Science

viz.note: 100 psychology studies, 2015

cards.hook: What if the failures never get published?
p: Studies with positive results are more likely to be published than those without, so the published record can look better than the truth. A review of 74 antidepressant trials registered with the US drug regulator found about half were positive. But in the published literature, 94% appeared positive.
Trial registration and publishing negative results are meant to fix this.
cards.ex: If ten teams test a useless idea and one gets a lucky result and publishes, readers see one success and none of the failures.
cards.k: Ask what was left out as well as what was reported.

q.q: What was the pattern in the antidepressant review?
o: Published studies looked more positive than all the trials
q.w: About 51% of all registered trials were positive, but the published literature made it look like 94% (Turner et al., 2008).

cards.src: Turner, Matthews, Linardatos, Tell & Rosenthal, 2008, New England Journal of Medicine

viz.note: 74 antidepressant trials, 2008 review

cards.h: What placebos can and cannot do
cards.hook: Can believing in a treatment make it work?
p: Expectation is powerful for things we feel and report, such as pain, nausea and fatigue. A large review of trials comparing placebo with no treatment found small effects on those, but no important effects on objective measures of disease.
A placebo can change how you feel without changing the illness underneath.
cards.ex: A sugar pill might ease a headache a little, but it will not shrink a tumour or clear an infection.
cards.k: Expectations can ease symptoms, but they do not cure disease.

q.q: What did the large review find about placebos?
o: Small effects on how we feel, little on objective outcomes
q.w: Hróbjartsson and Gøtzsche (2010) found modest effects on subjective outcomes such as pain, and little on objective ones.

cards.src: Hróbjartsson & Gøtzsche, 2010, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews

b: What can be measured: disease markers

cards.hook: How much should one surprising result change your mind?
p: Bayes’ rule is a way of updating a belief: your new confidence depends on how strong your prior belief was and how much more likely the new evidence is if the idea is true than if it is false.

A strong prior needs strong evidence to move it, which is the sense of the saying “extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence”. But evidence should move you in proportion, and in the right direction.
cards.ex: You have taken the same train for years and it is always on time. One late train should nudge your view, not overturn it.
cards.k: Move your belief in proportion to the strength of the evidence.

q.q: How should a single surprising result affect a well-supported belief?
o: It should nudge it in proportion to its strength
q.w: Bayesian updating shifts belief by an amount that depends on both the prior and how diagnostic the new evidence is.

cards.src: Bayes, 1763; Laplace, 1814

s: Ask: likely if true? if false?

cards.h: When a measure becomes a target
cards.hook: Why do targets so often backfire?
p: Goodhart’s law, in Marilyn Strathern’s phrasing, says that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. People start optimizing the number instead of the thing it was meant to represent.
The measure was useful because it tracked the goal; once it is rewarded, people find ways to move it without moving the goal.
cards.ex: Schools judged by test scores teach to the test, and call centers judged on call length hang up on callers sooner.
cards.k: Use a measure to learn, and be wary when it is also the target.

q.q: What does Goodhart’s law warn about?
o: A measure that becomes a target stops tracking the goal
q.w: Rewarding a number invites people to optimize it directly, which breaks its link to the goal.

cards.src: Goodhart, 1975; Strathern, 1997

cards.hook: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together. Does ice cream cause drowning?
p: Two things can move together without one causing the other. A third factor may drive both, as hot weather drives ice cream sales and swimming. Or the link may be chance, or run the other way.
To show cause, researchers use randomized trials where they can, or careful designs and several lines of evidence, such as the criteria Austin Bradford Hill set out in 1965.
cards.ex: Cities with more churches also have more crime, because both rise with population size.
cards.k: When two things move together, look for what drives both before blaming one on the other.

q.q: What best explains the ice cream and drowning link?
q.w: A shared cause, summer heat, raises both ice cream sales and swimming.

cards.src: Bradford Hill, 1965, Proceedings of the Royal Society of Medicine

cards.hook: Why is their mistake a flaw and yours a bad day?
p: We tend to explain other people’s behavior by their character and our own by our circumstances. In a classic study, readers who were told the writer had been assigned a position still judged that the essay reflected the writer’s real views.
The pull toward “that is just who they are” is strong, though it varies across cultures.
cards.ex: A driver cuts you off and you think “what a jerk.” When you cut someone off, it is because you were late and distracted.
cards.k: Before judging someone’s character, ask what situation might make a reasonable person act this way.

q.q: What is the fundamental attribution error?
o: Explaining others by character and overlooking the situation
q.w: We tend to read others’ behavior as showing who they are and neglect the pressures of the situation.

cards.src: Jones & Harris, 1967; Ross, 1977

a: “That is the kind of person they are”

cards.h: Four patterns that corrode a conversation
cards.hook: Which habits make arguments go downhill?
p: John Gottman’s observational studies of couples identified four habits that tend to go with deteriorating relationships: criticism of the person rather than the issue, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling. Contempt, such as mockery and eye-rolling, stood out as the most corrosive.
His claims about predicting outcomes come from small samples and are less precise than often reported, but the patterns are widely recognized by therapists.
cards.ex: “You never listen” attacks the person. “I felt ignored when I was speaking just now” describes the problem and your feeling.
cards.k: Describe the issue and your own feeling instead of attacking the person.

q.q: Which pattern did Gottman’s research flag as most corrosive?
q.w: In his observations contempt, which conveys disrespect, stood out as especially damaging, though prediction claims are overstated.

cards.src: Gottman & Levenson, 1992, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology; Gottman, 1994

b: A gentle start, appreciation, owning your part, a calming break

cards.hook: What makes someone feel understood?
p: Harry Reis and Phillip Shaver described closeness as built when one person feels understood, validated and cared for by another. Researchers call this perceived partner responsiveness, and it is a strong predictor of how close and satisfied people feel.
Techniques such as paraphrasing can help, but studies find they work best when sincere and accurate, and they do not always beat simple, warm acknowledgment.
cards.ex: Saying back “so you were worried it would look like you didn’t care” can show you really took it in, more than offering a fix.
cards.k: Show you understood before you try to solve it.

q.q: What does “perceived responsiveness” mean?
o: Feeling understood, validated and cared for by the other person
q.w: It is the sense that a partner gets, accepts and cares about you, and it is central to closeness.

cards.src: Reis & Shaver, 1988; Reis, Clark & Holmes, 2004

cards.hook: How do two people who want opposite things both win?
p: A position is what someone says they want; an interest is why. Roger Fisher and William Ury argued that negotiating over interests opens options that fighting over positions hides. Mary Parker Follett told of two people in a library, one wanting the window open and one closed.
Asking why revealed that one wanted fresh air and the other no draft on their neck, so they opened a window in the next room.
cards.ex: Two parents both insist on the same holiday. One wants rest, the other wants time with relatives. Several plans could give each of them what they actually want.
cards.k: Ask what the other person is really after, and say what you are after.

q.q: What does negotiating over interests mean?
o: Finding why each side wants what it wants
q.w: Interests are the reasons behind positions, and there are often more ways to meet them than the positions suggest.

cards.src: Follett, 1924; Fisher & Ury, 1981, Getting to Yes

cards.hook: Can asking someone for a favor make them like you more?
p: Benjamin Franklin wrote that a person who has once done you a kindness is more ready to do you another than someone you have obliged. In a 1969 experiment, people who were asked to return prize money as a personal favor rated the researcher more favorably than those who were not.
One explanation is that we justify our actions: “I helped, so I must like them.” Results since are mixed, so treat it as a tendency, not a trick.
cards.ex: Asking a neighbor to borrow a book can warm the relationship, as long as you return it and say thanks.
cards.k: Small, reasonable requests can build goodwill; manipulation breeds distrust.

q.q: What did the 1969 study find?
o: People liked those who had done them favors
People liked those they had done a favor for
q.w: Participants who did a personal favor for the researcher rated him more favorably (Jecker & Landy, 1969).

cards.src: Jecker & Landy, 1969, Human Relations

s: I justify it: “I must like them”

cards.hook: Why does a small gift make us feel we owe something?
p: People feel obliged to return favors, even small unrequested ones. In a 1971 experiment, a stranger who brought subjects a soft drink then asked them to buy raffle tickets, and they bought more than those who had received nothing, even if they did not like him.
It is a powerful social norm that salespeople and charities sometimes use.
cards.ex: Free samples and “gifts” in the mail can create an urge to give something back, even though you never asked for them.
cards.k: Notice the pull; you can accept a gift without owing a purchase.

q.q: What did the 1971 experiment show?
o: A favor increased later compliance, even without liking
q.w: Those who received a small unsolicited favor bought more raffle tickets, regardless of how much they liked the giver.

cards.src: Regan, 1971, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology; Cialdini, 2009

cards.hook: Would you contradict a room full of people about something obvious?
p: In Solomon Asch’s line-judgment experiments, participants matched the length of lines while confederates unanimously gave wrong answers. About three-quarters of participants went along with the group at least once, and about a third of all answers conformed.
When even one other person gave the correct answer, conformity dropped sharply.
cards.ex: In a meeting where everyone nods, one person saying “I am not sure about this” can free several others to say the same.
cards.k: One honest voice makes it easier for others to speak up.

q.q: What happened when someone else gave the correct answer?
q.w: Having a single ally substantially reduced conformity in Asch’s experiments.

cards.src: Asch, 1951; Asch, 1956, Psychological Monographs

viz.note: Asch line-judgment experiments

cards.hook: Does a crowd make us less likely to help?
p: In 1968 Darley and Latané staged a seizure over an intercom. When people thought they were alone with the victim, 85% reported it before the emergency ended; with four others they believed present, only 31% did. Responsibility spreads.
Later research adds nuance: the effect is weaker in clearly dangerous situations, and the famous story of the Kitty Genovese murder was exaggerated in early reports.
cards.ex: If you see someone in trouble in a crowd, pick one person and speak to them directly: “You, in the blue jacket, call 911.”
cards.k: In an emergency, do not assume someone else has acted; name a person and a task.

q.q: Who was most likely to report the seizure?
o: People who thought they were alone
q.w: Alone, 85% reported before the end; with four others believed present, 31% did (Darley & Latané, 1968).

cards.src: Darley & Latané, 1968; Fischer et al., 2011, Psychological Bulletin

viz.note: Reported the emergency before it ended, 1968

cards.hook: How little does it take to feel loyal to a group?
p: Henri Tajfel assigned people to groups on trivial grounds, such as which of two painters they preferred, or even by a coin toss. They then allocated points in a way that favored their own group over the other, though they would never meet and gained nothing.
Simply being sorted into “us” and “them” is enough to start favoritism.
cards.ex: Sports fans, office departments and school houses can feel fiercely loyal over very little.
cards.k: In-group favoritism comes cheap; watch for “us versus them” and look for what you share.

q.q: What did the minimal group studies show?
o: Arbitrary groups were enough to cause favoritism
Groups need real conflict to form
q.w: Even groups made on trivial or random grounds produced in-group favoritism in the point allocations.

cards.src: Tajfel, Billig, Bundy & Flament, 1971, European Journal of Social Psychology

viz.o: Trivial labels were enough to split people

cards.hook: Does getting to know people from another group help?
p: Gordon Allport proposed in 1954 that contact between groups reduces prejudice, most reliably when people have equal status, share goals, cooperate and have support from authorities. A review of 515 studies by Pettigrew and Tropp found that contact does tend to reduce prejudice.
The ideal conditions help but are not strictly needed, and contact works best when it is friendly and personal.
cards.ex: Working side by side on a shared project often changes opinions more than a lecture about tolerance.
cards.k: Cooperating on a shared goal tends to reduce prejudice.

q.q: What did the review of 515 studies find?
q.w: Pettigrew and Tropp (2006) found a consistent, modest reduction in prejudice with intergroup contact.

cards.src: Allport, 1954; Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

cards.hook: Does scrolling through other people’s lives make you feel worse?
p: Leon Festinger proposed in 1954 that people evaluate themselves by comparing with others. Comparing upward, with people who seem to be doing better, can lower mood and self-esteem; some experiments show this with social media profiles.
Large studies find the overall link between screen time and well-being is small, and effects differ by person and by how people use the platforms.
cards.ex: Seeing a friend’s highlight reel after a bad week can make your ordinary life look dull by comparison, when you are comparing your behind-the-scenes to their best moments.
cards.k: Compare your inside with your own past, not with other people’s outsides.

q.q: What do large studies find about screen use and well-being?
o: A small average link, varying by person
q.w: Orben and Przybylski (2019) found technology use explained very little of the variation in adolescent well-being.

cards.src: Festinger, 1954; Vogel et al., 2014; Orben & Przybylski, 2019, Nature Human Behaviour

viz.note: Share of variation in well-being linked to technology use was small

cards.hook: Why can’t you imagine how you will feel when you are in the grip of a feeling?
p: When calm, we underestimate how much anger, hunger, fear or desire will drive our behavior when we are in the grip of them, and when in the grip of them, we underestimate how we will think when calm. George Loewenstein calls it the hot–cold empathy gap.
In one study, people who were hungry chose to have more unhealthy snacks for the next week than people who had just eaten.
cards.ex: Sending an angry message feels right at 11 p.m. and mortifying at 9 a.m. Your calm self could have predicted that.
cards.k: Make big decisions when calm, and delay sending anything written in heat.

q.q: What is the empathy gap?
o: Failing to predict how a different emotional state will change you
q.w: It is the difficulty of imagining how a different visceral state, hot or cold, will affect your choices.

cards.src: Loewenstein, 1996, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes; Read & van Leeuwen, 1998

a: It feels obvious what to do

cards.h: We are more resilient than we predict
cards.hook: How long will you really feel that way?
p: People tend to overestimate how intensely and how long future events will affect their feelings, good or bad. In one study, assistant professors predicted that being denied tenure would hurt for years; later they were not much less happy than those who got it.
Daniel Gilbert suggests a kind of psychological immune system that works largely out of view, so we neglect it when we forecast.
cards.ex: You expect a setback to ruin the month; looking back, you find that daily life carried you along sooner than you expected.
cards.k: Expect your feelings to change; you are probably more adaptable than you predict.

q.q: What is the impact bias?
o: Overestimating how strongly and how long events will affect us
q.w: People tend to forecast feelings that are more intense and longer-lasting than those they actually have.

cards.src: Gilbert, Pinel, Wilson, Blumberg & Wheatley, 1998; Wilson & Gilbert, 2005

viz.note: Illustration of the direction of the finding

cards.hook: Do people like you more than you think?
p: After conversations with strangers, people consistently underestimate how much their partners liked them and enjoyed the conversation. Researchers call this the liking gap. Thoughtful self-critique after a chat, such as replaying what you said, may be part of why.
The gap showed up in the lab and between new roommates, where it persisted for months.
cards.ex: You leave a party sure you talked too much, while the other person went home thinking how easy you were to talk to.
cards.k: You are probably better liked than you assume; reach out anyway.

q.q: What did the liking gap studies find?
o: People overestimate how much others like them
People underestimate how much others like them after a conversation
q.w: Boothby and colleagues (2018) found people systematically underestimated their partners’ liking.

cards.src: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark, 2018, Psychological Science

viz.note: Direction of the finding, not exact data
